facts.claim: The sync and async client state enum distinguishes never-used, open, and closed clients; sending a request or entering a context opens it, while explicit close or context exit closes it.
pitfalls: Do not collapse unopened and closed into one state.
Context entry and request use both affect the open state.

facts.claim: A response-bound sync or async byte stream records elapsed time and closes its underlying stream when the consumer closes the response stream.
pitfalls: Elapsed time is set at close, not when response headers arrive.
Async and sync close paths await/use different underlying methods.

facts.claim: Client request construction merges URL, headers, cookies, and query parameters with client defaults, and uses the client timeout only when the per-request timeout selects the client-default sentinel and no timeout extension is already present.
pitfalls: An existing timeout extension bypasses default timeout insertion.
Per-request fields are merged rather than replacing every client default.

facts.claim: Relative request URLs are appended to a normalized base URL path after stripping a leading slash; absolute URLs pass through without that relative-path merge.
pitfalls: This is path append behavior, not ordinary root-relative URL resolution.
The base URL is normalized to end with a slash elsewhere in client setup.

facts.claim: Redirect handling checks the redirect-count limit, invokes request hooks before each network send, and invokes response hooks after each response, including responses that may lead to another redirect.
pitfalls: Hooks apply within redirect handling, not only once around the initial request.
The limit is checked for the current redirect history before sending.

facts.claim: Redirect request construction can rewrite the method and selectively adjust headers based on the destination, including removing authorization when the redirect changes host or scheme.
pitfalls: Redirects do not blindly reuse every original header.
Method rewriting depends on response status rules.

facts.claim: The base client maintains transport and client state, and rejects operations that require an open client after it has been closed.
pitfalls: State is distinct from whether the instance has merely been constructed.
Do not infer thread-safety from the state field.

facts.claim: The synchronous send path builds request/response handling around an injected transport and wraps the returned byte stream so response lifecycle metadata follows stream closure.
pitfalls: The send path is not equivalent to buffered get content handling.
The transport is called through the client lifecycle logic.

facts.claim: The asynchronous client has a separate async send and redirect path that awaits transport and hook operations rather than reusing the synchronous execution path.
pitfalls: AsyncClient behavior is not implemented by simply calling Client.send.
Hooks and stream closure have asynchronous counterparts.

facts.claim: Timeout configuration models connect, read, write, and pool phases, with a default timeout value that can be supplied as one number or component-specific values.
pitfalls: A timeout is not a single end-to-end wall-clock deadline.
Pool timeout is a separate phase from network connect/read/write.

facts.claim: ASGITransport adapts an async HTTP request into an ASGI HTTP scope and runs the application in-process, with request and response messages exchanged through the ASGI callable.
pitfalls: It is an in-process ASGI adapter, not a socket transport.
The scope and message exchange determine the request/response boundary.

facts.claim: The ASGI transport response stream yields the response body captured from ASGI send messages and terminates after the application reports completion.
pitfalls: Response body messages are distinct from response start metadata.
An application completion signal controls stream termination.

facts.claim: Signer accepts one or multiple secret keys ordered oldest to newest, signs with the newest key, and checks signatures against configured keys in reverse order to support rotation.
pitfalls: Verification order is newest-first even though storage order is oldest-first.
Old keys remain accepted until removed from configuration.

facts.claim: Signer rejects separators that overlap the base64 signature alphabet, then separates a signed value at its final separator occurrence so payloads may contain earlier separators.
pitfalls: The final separator is used when parsing.
Alphabet overlap is rejected at signer construction.

facts.claim: Signer derives a signing key from the secret and salt using a selected derivation scheme; supported branches include concat, django-concat, HMAC, and no derivation, and unknown schemes raise TypeError.
pitfalls: Key derivation is separate from the message signature algorithm.
The docs warn derivation is not a way to turn a short password into a strong secret.

facts.claim: The default HMAC signing algorithm verifies signatures with hmac.compare_digest against a freshly computed signature.
pitfalls: The compared bytes are the decoded signature and computed signature.
This mechanism does not make an insecure secret key strong.

facts.claim: Unsigning requires the configured separator, decodes and verifies the signature, returns the payload on success, and raises BadSignature when parsing or verification fails.
pitfalls: Missing separator and mismatched signature are distinct failure paths.
The error may retain the rejected payload as diagnostic data.

facts.claim: Serializer serializes an object to bytes, signs that payload, and on load verifies the signature before deserializing the payload back into an object.
pitfalls: A valid signature provides integrity/authenticity but does not encrypt the payload.
Deserialization follows signature verification.

facts.claim: Serializer passes its configured salt and signer configuration into the signer so tokens from separate signing contexts can be separated even when they share a secret key.
pitfalls: Salt is a context separation input, not a replacement for a secret key.
Changing salt makes existing signatures fail verification.

facts.claim: TimestampSigner appends a timestamp to signed data and validates it during unsign, raising a time-signature error when the timestamp is missing, malformed, future-dated, or older than the allowed age.
pitfalls: Timestamp verification is additional to signature verification.
An allowed max age is evaluated relative to current time.

facts.claim: TimedSerializer wraps serialized payloads in timestamped signatures and applies max_age during load while preserving the underlying serializer's payload conversion behavior.
pitfalls: Expiration is enforced on load, not by changing the encoded payload format into encryption.
The timestamped signer remains configurable.

facts.claim: URLSafeSerializer encodes serialized bytes into URL-safe base64 text before signing and reverses that encoding after successful load.
pitfalls: URL-safe encoding changes representation, not confidentiality.
Signing/verification remains part of the serializer flow.

facts.claim: The timed URL-safe serializer combines URL-safe payload representation with timestamp-based expiry checks through the timed serializer class hierarchy.
pitfalls: URL-safe and timed behaviors are composed through class inheritance.
Expiry still depends on max_age at load time.

facts.claim: Serializer loading may try configured fallback signer definitions after its primary signer fails, allowing explicit legacy signer settings during key or algorithm transitions.
pitfalls: Fallback acceptance is an explicit configuration decision.
Successful fallback verification does not rewrite or migrate the stored token.

facts.claim: parallel starts collection tasks without waiting for prior completion, but results retain collection order; a task error reaches the final callback immediately and tasks are not JavaScript CPU-parallel.
pitfalls: Parallel means overlapping asynchronous work rather than multiple JavaScript threads.
Result order follows input order rather than completion order.

facts.claim: waterfall requires an array, passes successful callback result arguments into the next task, and completes once a task errors or the final task finishes.
pitfalls: Only the first task begins without arguments.
The callback is guarded against multiple completion.

facts.claim: ensureAsync wraps callback-style functions so a synchronous callback is deferred to a later event-loop tick, while already-async functions are returned without an extra wrapper.
pitfalls: It does not force every callback to be deferred when already asynchronous.
The wrapper is intended to avoid recursive stack growth from synchronous callbacks.

facts.claim: memoize keys calls with a configurable hasher, coalesces concurrent calls for a missing key into a callback queue, and caches successful results but not errors.
pitfalls: Errors are deliberately not memoized.
Concurrent identical inputs share the active execution.

facts.claim: timeout reports an ETIMEDOUT error with optional info after its timer expires and ignores a later completion callback from the wrapped function.
pitfalls: The timeout wrapper does not cancel the underlying operation.
A late completion after timeout is suppressed.

facts.claim: queue defaults concurrency to one, rejects zero concurrency, and schedules queued work through a deferred process call while tracking active workers and queue lifecycle events.
pitfalls: Zero is rejected rather than treated as unlimited.
Task insertion schedules processing instead of running the worker inline.

facts.claim: The queue worker can receive batches controlled by payload, and task callbacks are removed from active-worker tracking when a batch completes.
pitfalls: Batch sizing and concurrency are separate controls.
A batch callback accounts for each task represented in the completed batch.

facts.claim: auto models named tasks and their dependencies, runs a task when its dependencies are satisfied subject to a concurrency bound, and returns keyed results.
pitfalls: Tasks with unresolved dependencies cannot start.
Dependency cycles are not valid execution plans.

facts.claim: retry controls the number and timing of task attempts, stops after success or exhaustion, and reports the final task result through its callback or promise interface.
pitfalls: The attempt limit includes the initial execution.
Retry behavior does not guarantee that the task is safe to repeat.

facts.claim: reflect converts a task completion into a result object containing either its error or successful result arguments, allowing aggregate flows to continue after individual failures.
pitfalls: The reflected task does not swallow the failure without recording it.
This permits a surrounding parallel collection to wait for other tasks.

facts.claim: eachOf iterates collection entries with their keys or indexes and provides the key to each iteratee, allowing object collections as well as indexed collections.
pitfalls: Iteration key is distinct from the item value.
Completion order does not imply iteration key order.

facts.claim: asyncify adapts a promise-returning or synchronous function to the library's callback convention, forwarding promise rejection or thrown errors as callback errors.
pitfalls: A returned promise rejection becomes an error-first callback result.
The adapter does not make a synchronous CPU function run in another thread.

facts.claim: ZodType.parse delegates to safeParse and throws its ZodError on failure, while safeParse returns a discriminated success/data or failure/error result after synchronous parsing.
pitfalls: safeParse does not throw validation failures as its normal result.
The synchronous path rejects a promise-returning parse operation.

facts.claim: safeParseAsync always establishes async parsing context and awaits either a synchronous parse result or a promise, while parseAsync throws the returned validation error on failure.
pitfalls: Async parsing supports schemas that contain async effects.
The async API does not change the success/error result shape.

facts.claim: ZodType tracks input and output types separately, allowing parsing transforms to accept one type and produce another type.
pitfalls: The inferred output type is not always the accepted input type.
Type tracking is separate from runtime validation behavior.

facts.claim: ZodObject parses declared keys and handles extra keys according to its unknown-key policy: strip omits them, passthrough retains them, and strict records an unrecognized-keys issue.
pitfalls: The default object mode is stripping, not strict rejection.
A catchall schema changes how extra keys are parsed.

facts.claim: Object shape composition preserves or explicitly carries unknown-key and catchall configuration when object schemas are extended or merged.
pitfalls: Shape extension is not simply a replacement of all object policy metadata.
Catchall behavior is independent of declared shape keys.

facts.claim: Array schemas encode ordinary arrays or non-empty tuple-like arrays in their output and input types, and validate exact, minimum, and maximum lengths before parsing elements.
pitfalls: Length constraints can make parsing fail before item checks.
At-least-one output has tuple shape rather than an unconstrained array type.

facts.claim: ZodUnion returns the first fully valid branch; if none is valid it prefers a dirty branch's issues, otherwise it constructs an invalid-union issue containing branch errors.
pitfalls: A dirty branch is not treated the same as a fully valid branch.
Union diagnostics retain per-branch validation errors when all branches are invalid.

facts.claim: Discriminated unions select an object branch by looking up its discriminator value in a precomputed option map and report a dedicated issue at the discriminator path when no option matches.
pitfalls: The discriminator must select a configured option.
This avoids reporting a generic union failure for an unmatched discriminator.

facts.claim: Effect schemas can preprocess input, refine parsed values, or transform values while carrying distinct input and output types through the type system.
pitfalls: Refinement checks validity while transform may change output value.
Async effects require async parsing APIs.

facts.claim: Default schemas substitute a configured default when the incoming value is undefined, then parse that substituted value through the wrapped schema.
pitfalls: Default is triggered by undefined rather than every falsy value.
The default value is still validated by the inner schema.

facts.claim: Lazy schemas defer retrieving their wrapped schema until parse time, allowing recursive schema definitions to refer to themselves.
pitfalls: The getter is evaluated through the lazy wrapper rather than at initial declaration.
Recursive schema construction does not itself validate recursive data.

facts.claim: Refinement APIs add custom validation issues to the shared parse context and can use a predicate or richer issue-producing callback to express constraints beyond built-in type checks.
pitfalls: A refinement failure is represented as a validation issue.
Async refinement logic requires asynchronous parsing.
